cues.text: A Vision of the Incomplete Moon
Juliana of Cornillon , born near Liège around 1192 and raised from childhood in the care of Augustinian canonesses, developed intense devotion to the Eucharist.
She reported a recurring vision of the full moon, brilliant but marked by a single dark gap — a sign she came to understand, after years of prayer, as representing the Church's liturgical year.
It was missing a feast dedicated entirely to Christ's presence in the Blessed Sacrament.
A Confidence Shared Cautiously
Juliana confided the vision first to her spiritual director and, in time, to Jacques Pantaléon , then archdeacon of Liège.
He took her conviction seriously; with his support, the Bishop of Liège, Robert de Thourotte, formally instituted a diocesan feast of Corpus Christi in 1246.
It was observed for the first time at the collegiate church of Saint-Martin in Liège five years later.
An Archdeacon Becomes Pope
Jacques Pantaléon was elected pope in 1261, taking the name Urban IV .

In 1264 — prompted, tradition holds, by both his memory of Juliana's vision and the Eucharistic sign reported that same decade at Bolsena — he extended the feast of Corpus Christi to the entire Catholic Church.
He did so through the bull Transiturus de hoc mundo , commissioning St. Thomas Aquinas to compose its liturgical texts.
A Date This Entry Cannot Fully Account For
The Church's own exhibition of Eucharistic miracles labels this account “Liège, 1374.”
That date does not correspond to any specific event in the documented history of Juliana's visions.
It also does not correspond to the 1246 diocesan feast or Urban IV's 1264 bull, all of which took place a century earlier.
This entry presents the well-documented Liège origins of Corpus Christi plainly, but flags the specific 1374 date as unresolved rather than invent an explanation for it.
Legacy

Liège's own devotion to the feast it helped originate has continued, with interruptions, for over seven centuries; a lay association revived the city's Corpus Christi procession in the twenty-first century after it had lapsed for decades.
Juliana herself, canonized only informally through centuries of local veneration before her sacred devotion was formally confirmed.
She remains honored across the Catholic world as the quiet originator of one of the Church's most widely celebrated Eucharistic feasts.
